lead: Pennsylvania has old homes, river floods and hurricane remnants. DryFlare helps owners from Philadelphia to Pittsburgh and the Lehigh Valley get water out fast.
risk: river and flash flooding, old plumbing and frozen pipes
risk_short: flash floods, old pipes, frozen pipes
why: A quarter of Pennsylvania homes went up before 1940. Philly rowhomes and Pittsburgh's hillside houses often have old drains, stone basements and iron pipes. Basements take water in heavy rain. Old pipes freeze in deep cold.

Remnants of hurricanes cause major floods here. Ida flooded the Schuylkill River and towns like Bridgeport and Norristown in 2021. Tropical Storm Debby flooded north-central Pennsylvania in 2024. River towns still remember Agnes in 1972. New Jersey and Ohio share many of these storms.
image_alt: Water standing on a basement floor after a storm
image_caption: Stone basements in older Pennsylvania homes often take on water during heavy rain.
tips: Seal cracks in stone basement walls and keep gutters clear.
Install a backwater valve if your basement has a floor drain.
Keep heat on in vacant rental units over winter.
Know your flood zone if you live near a river or stream.
insurance: Most Pennsylvania home policies exclude sewer backup and sump pump failure. You can add water backup cover.

faq.q: How fast should a flooded Pennsylvania basement be dried?
faq.a: Start within 24 to 48 hours to stop mold. Pump out the water, pull wet carpet and drywall, and run dehumidifiers. Stone and block walls hold water, so drying can take several days. Moisture readings show when it is done.

licensing: Pennsylvania has no statewide general contractor license. But most home improvement contractors must register with the Attorney General's Office. Philadelphia and Pittsburgh also license contractors.
licensing_faq: Home improvement contractors must register with the Pennsylvania Attorney General's Office. Some cities, such as Philadelphia, require local licenses too.
